structured.options_hint: Syntactic Semantic Collocation None of t

items.explanation: In Gerard Manley Hopkins's sonnet "As Kingfishers Catch Fire," the clause "The just man justices" turns the adjective/noun "just" into a verb ("justices"), creating syntactic (and semantic) foregrounding; UGC accepted both (A) and (B).

items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit II: Poetry · Edmund Spenser

in

medieval works of literature and art

structured.lead: The separation of styles in accordance with class appears more consistently in _______ than in medieval works of literature and art
structured.options_hint: Ben Jonson Shakespeare Philip Sidney Edm

items.explanation: In Mimesis: The Representation of Reality in Western Literature (1946), Erich Auerbach observes that the separation of styles according to social class—where noble characters speak in elevated verse and lower-class characters in comic prose—appears more consistently in Shakespeare than in medieval literature.

items.stem:

This coyness, lady, were no crime."
This statement is an example of

structured.lead:
"Had we but world enough, and time,
This coyness, lady, were no crime."
This statement is an example of
structured.options_hint: Irony Paradox Hyperbole Euphemism

items.explanation: Taken from the opening couplet of Andrew Marvell's metaphysical poem "To His Coy Mistress" (1681), this conditional statement uses irony and mock-serious understatement to gently critique the lady's modesty before contrasting it with human mortality.

items.stem: A Spenserian stanza has

structured.lead: A Spenserian stanza has
structured.options_hint: four iambic pentameters six iambic penta

items.explanation: Invented by Edmund Spenser for his epic poem The Faerie Queene (1590–1596), the Spenserian stanza consists of nine lines: eight lines in iambic pentameter followed by a single alexandrine (iambic hexameter), rhyming ababbcbcc.

items.title: Q9 · June 2014 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
"The greatness of a poet", Arnold says,
"lies in his powerful and beautiful
application of ideas to life". But a
critic pointed out it was "not a happy
way of putting it, as if ideas were a
lotion for the inflamed skin of
suffering humanity". Who was this
critic ?

structured.lead:
"The greatness of a poet", Arnold says,
"lies in his powerful and beautiful application of ideas to life". But a critic pointed out it was "not a happy way of putting it, as if ideas were a lotion for the inflamed skin of suffering humanity". Who was this critic ?
structured.options_hint: Eliot Leavis David Lodge Allen Tate

items.explanation: In The Use of Poetry and the Use of Criticism (1933), T. S. Eliot critiques Matthew Arnold's definition of poetry from his essay "Wordsworth" (1879), remarking that Arnold's phrasing makes ideas sound like an external lotion applied to the inflamed skin of suffering humanity.

structured.lead:

structured.options_hint: lyrics epics sonnets stanzas

items.explanation: In John Donne's metaphysical poem "The Canonization" (1633), the speaker declares that even if their love is unfit for grand historical chronicles, they will "build in sonnets pretty rooms," playing on the Italian word stanza (meaning "room").

structured.lead:
The son of a joiner, he was apprenticed as a printer. He remained
a printer throughout his life. He was asked to prepare a series of modern letters for those who could not write for themselves. This humble task taught him the art of expressing himself in letters. Who is the novelist ?
structured.options_hint: Daniel Defoe Samuel Richardson Henry Fie

items.explanation: Samuel Richardson (1689–1761), the son of a joiner and a master printer by trade, was commissioned in 1739 to write a volume of model letters for country readers, which directly inspired his pioneering epistolary novel Pamela; or, Virtue Rewarded (1740).

items.explanation: Although William Wordsworth began The Prelude in 1798–1799 and completed the 13-book version in 1805, he continued revising it throughout his life, and it was published posthumously in 14 books in 1850 shortly after his death.
